Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I can't rely on other people

issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: 'Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of natural disaster. A car-crash-specific trigger suggests a different index trauma unless there is clear disaster-related context, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: 'Rage on Recall' is not well supported by the rest of the profile, which otherwise centers on fear, vulnerability, dissociation/gaps, and interpersonal mistrust after a natural disaster. Intense rage could occur clinically, but here it lacks corroboration from threat or appraisal items and weakens overall coherence.

For a natural disaster trauma, 'related people' as a primary trigger is hard to justify unless they were directly linked to the event; with no supporting interpersonal trauma content elsewhere, this trigger is clinically questionable.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
issues.explanation: The threat item about unusual silence implying imminent danger fits combat/interpersonal danger contexts more than natural disaster exposure, and it is not supported by the trigger or appraisal content here.

vignette:
Ethan, a 29-year-old European American man who worked in sales, had been camping alone in a wooded area near a lake when the storm hit. He had gone there for a weekend to clear his head after a difficult stretch at work, choosing the site because it felt quiet and open, away from phones and obligations. Late that evening the weather turned with little warning. He remembered the sky shifting dark, the wind picking up through the trees, and then the frightening rush of realizing how quickly the water around him was rising. In the aftermath, when he tried to explain what had happened, there were parts he simply could not account for no matter how many times he went over the sequence in his mind. What he could remember returned with the same terror he had felt in the moment: the panic, the helplessness, the sense that he was exposed in a place that had seemed peaceful only hours earlier. Even months later, he would sometimes be overtaken by the full force of that dread without seeing a clear picture in his mind, as if the fear itself came first and the memory followed behind.

At first Ethan tried to treat the experience as something he should be able to put behind him, but the days after the storm brought a lasting sense that he no longer knew himself in the same way. He had once seen himself as self-sufficient and steady, yet now he felt unsettled by his own reactions and embarrassed by how easily he startled or checked his surroundings. He came to believe he could not rely on other people in the way he once had, and that belief grew sharper whenever he thought about how alone he had been when the weather changed. Friends offered reassurance, but he found himself keeping them at a distance, not because he wanted to be difficult, but because trusting anyone else to notice danger in time felt naïve to him. Over the months, he also found that nothing in his life felt especially meaningful anymore. He continued to go through the motions of work and errands, but the sense of purpose he had once attached to his plans had thinned, leaving him feeling as though he was moving through days that no longer quite belonged to him.

Certain situations brought the experience rushing back in immediate, bodily ways. Being in natural environments similar to the place where it happened was especially hard, and he began to avoid the lakefront and wooded trails he had once liked. Even driving past physical locations that resembled the campsite could make his body tense before he had fully registered why. At work, as a salesperson, he spent much of his day moving between offices, storefronts, and parking lots, and he noticed that any unfamiliar open space could leave him on edge, scanning exits and weather conditions with a vigilance that exhausted him. He became especially unsettled when he felt emotionally vulnerable, because that state seemed to strip away whatever control he could muster. In those moments he was more likely to feel as if the danger were close again, and his mind could slip into brief flashback-like states in which he suddenly acted as though the storm were returning, looking around sharply or freezing in place before he could fully orient himself.

At night, Ethan rarely slept without disruption. He would wake during the night to check whether he was safe, sometimes sitting upright and listening for sounds that would tell him he was in danger. He kept a charged phone nearby, checked weather alerts more often than he wanted to admit, and would get up to look out the window if the wind changed. During the day he remained superalert, watching the sky, the trees, and the people around him in a way that made it difficult to settle into ordinary routines. The pattern had begun to affect his work as a salesperson in quieter but unmistakable ways: he arrived tired, found it harder to concentrate during client meetings, and sometimes shortened conversations so he could get back to the familiar security of indoor spaces. What finally brought him to seek help was the accumulation of these nights and days, and the growing fear that he was becoming someone entirely unfamiliar to himself. He said he wanted to sleep without waking in a panic, to walk outside without feeling as if the air itself might turn against him, and to find some way to live that did not feel stripped of meaning.
